## 7. Migrating from B2 / legacy `HarborConfig`

### 7.1 B2 → C1 (per-app common fields → CommonConfig)

Before task C1, `AppConfigBase` declared the common fields directly:

```csharp
// B2 layout — DEPRECATED
public abstract record AppConfigBase {
    public string Theme { get; init; } = "dark";
    public string LogLevel { get; init; } = "info";
    public string LastUsedProvider { get; init; } = "";
    public string LastUsedModel { get; init; } = "";
    public string LastUsedAgent { get; init; } = "code";
    public ImmutableList<string> RecentSessions { get; init; } = ...;
}
```

Each per-app JSON file duplicated these fields, so changing one app's
`LogLevel` didn't affect the others. Task C1 moved them all to
`CommonConfig` (~/.harbor/config.json) so they're shared.

**Migration path (manual, not auto-applied):**

1. The user launches any app under task C1 for the first time.
2. `JsonCommonConfigStore.LoadAsync()` finds `~/.harbor/config.json` either
   missing (first-ever run) or containing the legacy `HarborConfig` JSON
   (provider/model/apiKeys/...).
3. The legacy `HarborConfig` and the new `CommonConfig` JSON shapes overlap
   on the `apiKeys` / `LogLevel` / `Storage` / `Compaction*` fields but use
   different casing / property names. `JsonCommonConfigStore` does NOT
   auto-migrate — it loads whatever fields it can map and uses defaults for
   the rest.
4. The user can run `harbor config migrate` (planned, not yet implemented) to
   copy the orphaned common fields from each `<app>.json` into
   `config.json` and zero them out in the per-app files. Auto-migration is
   intentionally NOT done at startup — it's risky and reversible only by
   hand.

**What to do today:** if you have a `~/.harbor/cli.json` from B2 with
`LogLevel` / `Theme` / `LastUsedProvider` / `LastUsedModel` / `LastUsedAgent`
/ `RecentSessions` fields, those fields are now silently ignored by the CLI
(JsonAppConfigStore<CliConfig> no longer has those properties to
deserialize into). The CLI falls back to CommonConfig defaults. To preserve
the user's intent, manually copy those values to `~/.harbor/config.json`:

```bash
# Example: copy LogLevel from cli.json to config.json
jq -s '.[0].LogLevel = .[1].LogLevel | .[0]' config.json cli.json > config.json.new
mv config.json.new config.json
```

### 7.2 Legacy `HarborConfig` (still in use)

The legacy `HarborConfig` (`src/Harbor.PolicyConfig/Configuration/HarborConfig.cs`)
still exists at `~/.harbor/config.json`. It owns:

- API keys per provider (used by `AuthStore`)
- Custom provider configs (overrides the bundled JSON presets)
- Enabled plugins
- Disabled builtin tools
- Default max steps per agent run
- Repeat-guard threshold per agent run
- Cost limit per session
- Compaction settings
- The per-plugin configuration sections (`plugins.<plugin-id>`)

### The per-plugin sections

`plugins.<plugin-id>` holds a plugin's OWN settings, and nothing else. The
plugin declares them in its manifest, and the host checks the user's values
against that declaration before the plugin starts:

```json
{
  "plugins": {
    "web-search": { "maxResults": 10 }
  }
}
```

A setting the user did not set carries the default the schema published, so a
plugin always reads a value. A setting the plugin declares no default for is
required: the plugin does not start until the user gives it a value. The
section is stored exactly as the user wrote it, because what a section means is
the plugin's schema and the schema travels with the plugin. See
[PLUGIN_SYSTEM.md §The plugin's own settings](./PLUGIN_SYSTEM.md#the-plugins-own-settings-1734).

**`maxSteps` is the step budget of a run.** The value is how many LLM turns an
agent run may take: the loop stops at exactly that many turns and the run says
it was cut off by the budget (`RunLimitKind.MaxSteps`) instead of pretending it
finished. The budget is projected onto the agent the run starts with, so it
holds for every entry point — the interactive REPL, `harbor ask` and
`harbor run task` alike. It is read when the process starts, so a change to
the key takes effect on the next start of Harbor (like `storage` and `tui`).
A value equal to the built-in default (50) means "no budget configured": each
agent then keeps its own step budget (`code`, `ask` and `debug` 50; `plan`,
`architect` and `orchestrator` 100; `explore` 20), which is what every install
that never touched the key has — 50 is the value every config save writes into
the file, so honouring it as an override would silently halve the 100-step
agents for users who never asked for it. Any other value is the budget of the
run. See issue #1118.

**`repeatToolThreshold` is the repeat guard's threshold.** The value is how
many CONSECUTIVE identical tool calls (the same tool, the same arguments) may
happen before the model is told that it is repeating itself. The guard is
advisory: the call still runs, the run is never ended by it — it only puts a
reminder in front of the repeated call's result, so the agent gets a chance to
change its mind before the step budget or the token budget runs out. `0` turns
the guard off; the default (3) is the value every install runs with, and a
config that carries it says nothing the agent's own value does not. Like
`maxSteps`, the value is projected onto the agent the run starts with, so it
holds for every entry point, and it is read when the process starts. See
issue #1756.

**Important:** task C1 RE-PURPOSED the `~/.harbor/config.json` path for
`CommonConfig`. Both `HarborConfig` and `CommonConfig` are now reading/writing
the SAME file. The two types overlap on the `apiKeys` / `LogLevel` /
`Storage` / `Compaction*` fields (System.Text.Json is case-insensitive in
web-default mode, so `apiKeys` and `ApiKeys` deserialize to the same
property). Fields unique to one type are ignored by the other's loader.

| Concern | Lives in (during migration) | File |
| --- | --- | --- |
| API keys, provider presets, compaction, cost limits | `HarborConfig` (legacy `IConfigStore`) | `~/.harbor/config.json` |
| Default provider / model / agent (SHARED) | `CommonConfig` (new) | `~/.harbor/config.json` |
| Storage backend (SHARED) | `CommonConfig` (new) | `~/.harbor/config.json` |
| Logging (SHARED) | `CommonConfig` (new) | `~/.harbor/config.json` |
| CLI UX (TUI renderer, onboarding, history) | `CliConfig` | `~/.harbor/cli.json` |
| Avalonia UX (window, fonts, panels) | `AvaloniaConfig` | `~/.harbor/avalonia.json` |
| WPF UX (window, AvalonDock) | `WpfConfig` | `~/.harbor/wpf.json` |
| MAUI UX (dark mode, last platform) | `MauiConfig` | `~/.harbor/maui.json` |
| Blazor UX (listen port, browser-launch) | `BlazorConfig` | `~/.harbor/blazor.json` |
| Theme tokens (shared across desktop apps) | `ThemeManager` | `~/.harbor/theme.json` |
| Session transcripts (shared across all apps) | `JsonlSessionStore` | `~/.harbor/sessions/*.jsonl` |

### 7.3 Future migration (consolidate)

If a future sprint wants to fold `HarborConfig` entirely into `CommonConfig`:

1. Move the remaining legacy fields (`Provider`/`Model`/`Agent`/`Onboarded`/
   `Tui`/`Storage`/`MaxSteps`/`CostLimit`/`EnabledPlugins`/`DisabledTools`/
   `Providers`) into `CommonConfig`.
2. Update `AuthStore` + `OnboardingWizard` + `ConfigCommand` to take
   `ICommonConfigStore` instead of `IConfigStore`.
3. Provide a `harbor config migrate` CLI command that copies orphaned fields
   from per-app JSONs into `config.json` and writes a `.bak` of the original.
4. Delete `HarborConfig` + `JsonConfigStore` + `IConfigStore` once no
   production code references them.

This is OUT OF SCOPE for task C1 — it's a follow-up.

## 8. Example JSON files

### `~/.harbor/config.json` (CommonConfig — SHARED)

```json
{
  "configVersion": "1",
  "apiKeys": {
    "anthropic": "sk-ant-xxx",
    "openai": "sk-proj-yyy"
  },
  "defaultProvider": "anthropic",
  "defaultModel": "claude-sonnet-4",
  "defaultAgent": "code",
  "storageBackend": "jsonl",
  "storagePath": "",
  "logLevel": "info",
  "enableFileLogging": true,
  "maxLogFiles": 50,
  "permissionMode": "default",
  "alwaysAllowTools": [],
  "alwaysDenyTools": [],
  "enablePlugins": true,
  "pluginDirectories": "",
  "enableScripting": true,
  "httpProxy": "",
  "httpTimeoutSeconds": 30,
  "userAgent": "Harbor/0.7",
  "compactionReserveTokens": 16384,
  "compactionKeepRecentTokens": 20000,
  "compactionTailTurns": 2
}
```

### `~/.harbor/cli.json` (CliConfig — CLI-specific ONLY)

```json
{

  "enableOnboardingWizard": false,
  "enableSlashCommands": true,

}
```

### `~/.harbor/avalonia.json` (AvaloniaConfig — Avalonia-specific ONLY)

---

## 9. Architecture

```
Harbor.Desktop.Abstractions/Configuration/
├── AppConfigBase.cs           ← abstract record (path plumbing ONLY — no common fields)
├── IAppConfigStore.cs         ← per-app repository contract (Result<T> returns)
├── JsonAppConfigStore.cs      ← per-app JSON impl (atomic write + SemaphoreSlim)
├── CommonConfig.cs            ← NEW (C1): sealed record, shared across every app
├── ICommonConfigStore.cs      ← NEW (C1): shared repository contract
├── JsonCommonConfigStore.cs   ← NEW (C1): JSON impl for CommonConfig
└── CompositeConfig.cs         ← NEW (C1): pairs CommonConfig + TAppConfig for DI

apps/Harbor.App.Cli/Configuration/CliConfig.cs         ← sealed record : AppConfigBase
apps/Harbor.App.Avalonia/Configuration/AvaloniaConfig.cs
contrib/apps/Harbor.App.Wpf/Configuration/WpfConfig.cs
contrib/apps/Harbor.App.Maui/Configuration/MauiConfig.cs
contrib/apps/Harbor.App.Blazor/Configuration/BlazorConfig.cs
```

Each app's composition root wires BOTH layers:

```csharp
// Shared layer (~/.harbor/config.json)
builder.Services.AddSingleton<ICommonConfigStore>(sp =>
    new JsonCommonConfigStore(
        new CommonConfig(),
        sp.GetRequiredService<ILogger<JsonCommonConfigStore>>()));
builder.Services.AddSingleton(sp =>
{
    var store = sp.GetRequiredService<ICommonConfigStore>();
    var result = store.LoadAsync().GetAwaiter().GetResult();
    return result.IsSuccess ? result.Value : new CommonConfig();
});

// App-specific layer (~/.harbor/<app>.json)
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IAppConfigStore<TAppConfig>>(sp =>
    new JsonAppConfigStore<TAppConfig>(
        new TAppConfig(),
        sp.GetRequiredService<ILogger<JsonAppConfigStore<TAppConfig>>>()));
builder.Services.AddSingleton(sp =>
{
    var store = sp.GetRequiredService<IAppConfigStore<TAppConfig>>();
    var result = store.LoadAsync().GetAwaiter().GetResult();
    return result.IsSuccess ? result.Value : new TAppConfig();
});

// Convenience pair for services that need fields from BOTH layers
builder.Services.AddSingleton<CompositeConfig<TAppConfig>>(sp =>
    new CompositeConfig<TAppConfig>(
        sp.GetRequiredService<CommonConfig>(),
        sp.GetRequiredService<TAppConfig>()));
```

The eager `LoadAsync` calls at startup populate the `CommonConfig` +
`TAppConfig` singletons that the rest of the composition root resolves
synchronously.

### Thread safety

- `JsonCommonConfigStore` uses a single `SemaphoreSlim(1, 1)` to serialize
  Load/Save/Update. Concurrent callers block on the semaphore.
- `JsonAppConfigStore<T>` uses the same pattern.
- The `CommonConfig` / `TAppConfig` singletons registered in DI are snapshots —
  they do NOT reflect writes from other processes. To pick up external writes,
  call `store.LoadAsync()` again.

### Atomicity

- `SaveAsync` writes to `<file>.tmp` first, then `File.Move` into place.
- On POSIX, `File.Move` is atomic when the destination doesn't exist;
  `SaveAsync` deletes the destination first if it exists.
- On Windows, `File.Move` with `File.Delete` first is the documented atomic-
  replace pattern (the .NET runtime does NOT expose `MoveFileEx` with
  `MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING` directly).
- A crash mid-write leaves the previous file intact (the temp file is
  orphaned but does NOT corrupt the destination).

---

## 10. DI tests

Each app's test project asserts that BOTH `ICommonConfigStore` + `CommonConfig`
(shared) AND `IAppConfigStore<TAppConfig>` + `TAppConfig` (app-specific) AND
`CompositeConfig<TAppConfig>` (composite) are registered
(Wpf/Maui/Blazor test projects live in `contrib/tests/` since sprint-2):

| Test project | Test file | Assertions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Harbor.App.Cli.Tests` | `HostBuilderDiTests.cs` | `ICommonConfigStore`, `CommonConfig`, `CompositeConfig<CliConfig>`, `IAppConfigStore<CliConfig>`, `CliConfig` |
| `Harbor.App.Avalonia.Tests` | `AppHostDiTests.cs` | `ICommonConfigStore`, `CommonConfig`, `CompositeConfig<AvaloniaConfig>`, `IAppConfigStore<AvaloniaConfig>`, `AvaloniaConfig` |
| `Harbor.App.Wpf.Tests` | `AppDiTests.cs` | `ICommonConfigStore`, `CommonConfig`, `CompositeConfig<WpfConfig>`, `IAppConfigStore<WpfConfig>`, `WpfConfig` |
| `Harbor.App.Maui.Tests` | `MauiProgramDiTests.cs` | `ICommonConfigStore`, `CommonConfig`, `CompositeConfig<MauiConfig>`, `IAppConfigStore<MauiConfig>`, `MauiConfig` |
| `Harbor.App.Blazor.Tests` | `ProgramDiTests.cs` | `ICommonConfigStore`, `CommonConfig`, `CompositeConfig<BlazorConfig>`, `IAppConfigStore<BlazorConfig>`, `BlazorConfig` |

Each test class also has an aggregate `Build_AllDeclaredServices_Resolvable`

with the actual registrations.

---

## 11. Future work

- **`harbor config migrate` CLI command** — copy orphaned common fields from
  each `<app>.json` into `config.json` and zero them out in the per-app
  files. Auto-migration at startup is intentionally NOT done (risky); the
  command makes it a one-step opt-in.
- **Fold `HarborConfig` into `CommonConfig`** — move the remaining legacy
  fields (`Provider`/`Model`/`Agent`/`Onboarded`/`Tui`/`Storage`/`MaxSteps`/
  `CostLimit`/`EnabledPlugins`/`DisabledTools`/`Providers`) into
  `CommonConfig` and update `AuthStore` + `OnboardingWizard` +
  `ConfigCommand` to take `ICommonConfigStore`. See §7.3 above.
- **Per-app config UI** — `SettingsView` in Avalonia/WPF/Blazor should
  surface the per-app fields as editable forms. Currently the Settings VM
  reads from the legacy `HarborConfig`; switch it to the app's per-app
  config record + the shared `CommonConfig`.
- **Schema validation** — currently `LoadAsync` falls back to defaults on
  JSON parse errors. Add a JSON-schema validator that surfaces specific
  field errors to the user (e.g. "StorageBackend must be one of
  jsonl/sqlite/memory").
- **Encrypted secrets** — `CommonConfig.ApiKeys` currently stores API keys
  in plaintext. They should be encrypted via the OS keychain (DPAPI on
  Windows, Keychain on macOS, Secret Service on Linux). Separate concern,
  tracked separately.
- **Cross-app realtime sync** — when the user changes `DefaultProvider` in
  one app, the other apps should pick it up on next launch. Currently each
  app reads `~/.harbor/config.json` once at startup; if realtime sync is
  desired, add a `FileSystemWatcher` to `JsonCommonConfigStore` that
  reloads the singleton on external writes.

# Session file format

What a session file is, which generation of the format it is in, and what a
reader does with a file whose generation it does not know.

The session file is a public artifact. It is what the session picker lists,
what the export copies, and, in the keyless tier (#1740), what a repository
carries, because a log written in that tier holds no provider credential. A
change to its shape is therefore a change to a contract, and this document is
where that contract is written down.

- The code: [../src/Harbor.Storage.Jsonl/SessionFormatCatalog.cs](../src/Harbor.Storage.Jsonl/SessionFormatCatalog.cs) (the generations), [../src/Harbor.Storage.Jsonl/SessionFormatMigrations.cs](../src/Harbor.Storage.Jsonl/SessionFormatMigrations.cs) (the chain), [../src/Harbor.Storage.Jsonl/SessionStoreRecords.cs](../src/Harbor.Storage.Jsonl/SessionStoreRecords.cs) (the header record).
- The corpus: [../tests/Harbor.Storage.Jsonl.Tests/fixtures/](../tests/Harbor.Storage.Jsonl.Tests/fixtures/) — one committed file per generation.
- The tests: [../tests/Harbor.Storage.Jsonl.Tests/SessionFormatCorpusTests.cs](../tests/Harbor.Storage.Jsonl.Tests/SessionFormatCorpusTests.cs).

## The file

One session is one file, `<sessionId>.jsonl`, under the store's directory.
Line 1 is the header; the lines after it are the records, in the order they
were written.

```json
{"type":"session","version":1,"formatVersion":1,"id":"…","projectId":"…","directory":"…","title":"…","agent":"…","model":"…","providerId":"…","createdAt":"…","updatedAt":"…","parentSessionId":null,"status":0,"gitBranch":null,"gitIsDirty":false,"kind":0}
{"type":"message","id":"…","parentId":null,"role":"user","createdAt":"…","payload":{…}}
{"type":"checkpoint","id":"…","messageId":"…","messageIndex":0,"createdAt":"…","label":null,"rewindOf":null,"removed":0}
{"type":"messageRating","id":"…","messageId":"…","rating":"Helpful","category":"TaskResult","createdAt":"…","note":null}
{"type":"sessionRemark","id":"…","text":"…","createdAt":"…"}
{"type":"goal","objective":"…","phase":"Active","maxRounds":3,"roundsStarted":1,"revision":2,"createdAt":"…","updatedAt":"…","blockedReason":null,"blockedCode":null}
```

There are five record kinds. A `message` is what the model reads. The other
four are not history: a `checkpoint` is a rewind marker (#1247), a
`messageRating` is the user's rating of one message, a `sessionRemark` is
free text about the session (#1746), and a `goal` is a snapshot of the
session's durable goal — the phase, the round budget and the counter of the
work the session is doing (#1761). The message read path skips all four,
which is what makes "the feedback never reaches the model" a property of the
format rather than a promise.

### The header's two versions

The header carries two version fields, and they answer different questions.

| Field | Question it answers | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | Which shape is this header record? | `1`, since the first commit of the store |
| `formatVersion` | Which generation of the session format is this file? | `1` in every file this build writes |

`formatVersion` is the generation of the whole contract, header and records
together. It is absent in a file written before the marker existed.

## The generations

| Generation | Header | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| V0 (legacy) | no `formatVersion` | written before the format was versioned |
| V1 (current) | `"formatVersion":1` | what this build writes |

V1 is the current generation and it is generation 1, not generation 4,
because the format grew three times already and every one of those growths
was additive:

- the feedback records (#1746) added a record kind and changed no record that
  already existed;
- the keyless marker (#1740) added a header field and changed no record that
  already existed;
- the transcript contract (#1806) added a reader's view, derived in memory
  rather than stored.

The goal records (#1761) are the fourth such growth, and the same shape: a
record kind of their own, no record that already existed changed. A file
written before the goal axis existed is still a V1 file — it simply has no
goal line, and their absence is not a malformed line.

An extension that had needed a retroactive migration would have shown up as a
second generation, with a migration step and a fixture of its own. None did,
so V1 covers every file the store has ever written, except the ones written
before the marker existed.

## The migration chain

A file is read through the chain from its own generation to the current one.
The chain is walked one generation at a time, so the order of the steps is
the order of the generations.

| Step | What it does |
|---|---|
| V0 to V1 | the header gains the format marker, and the last-activity stamp a V0 header cannot state is materialized from the file's own write time |

Every other field the V1 generation states is already at its V1 value in a
V0 header, because a V0 header simply did not state it. The reader has been
filling the V1 defaults in since the day those fields were added, so the
migration changes the header's shape and not what a caller sees.

The rules the chain obeys:

- **A step is idempotent.** Applied to a header that already carries the
  marker and a stamp, it returns the same header.
- **A gap is an error, not a guess.** A generation with no step fails the
  read with "this build has no migration from that generation".
- **The writer always writes the current generation.** So the first header
  rewrite upgrades a legacy file on disk, and a file this build writes is
  never a legacy file.

## A file this build does not read

A file whose generation is above the current one is refused, everywhere it
could be read: the session record, the message history, the feedback records
and the checkpoint markers. The refusal names the version:

```
Session 'abc' is written in session format version 2, which this build does not read (it reads up to version 1): /home/u/.harbor/sessions/abc.jsonl.
```

The listing is the one path that cannot refuse, because one unreadable file
must not empty the session picker. It skips the file and says so in the log,
with the same reason.

A session file is read as a whole or not at all. Reading half of a file whose
meaning this build does not have is how records go missing without a word.

## The corpus

Every generation has a committed fixture, and every step of the chain is
covered by the fixture of the generation it reads. A migration nothing
exercises is a migration nobody knows works.

| Generation | Fixture | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| V0 | `session-format-v0-legacy.jsonl` | a header that states no generation and none of the V1 fields, plus two message records |
| V1 | `session-format-v1-current.jsonl` | a header that states the generation, two message records, a checkpoint and a rating |

The fixtures live in
[../tests/Harbor.Storage.Jsonl.Tests/fixtures/](../tests/Harbor.Storage.Jsonl.Tests/fixtures/)
and are read from the checkout, the way the other test fixtures in this
repository are read. A fixture's file name is the session id inside it, so a
fixture copied into a store's directory is found under the name the store
looks it up by.

The policy is a test, not a promise:
`EveryGenerationInTheCatalog_HasACommittedFixture` fails when a generation is
declared without a fixture, and `EveryMigrationStep_IsCoveredByAFixture`
fails when a step reads a generation the corpus does not cover.

## The other backends

The SQLite backend has its own schema and evolves on its own path
(`SqliteSchema`); its `version` column holds the product version, not a
format generation. The memory backend has no file at all. The contract on
this page is the JSONL session file's, and the two backends are not compared
across formats.

# CI gates: the policy for the python tools in `tools/`

This document says three things:

1. why the gates in `tools/` are python and not C#,
2. what the compiler takes over, and what stays in python because the compiler
   cannot see it,
3. what every gate owes the repository, and what a gate must not do.

The last one is not prose with nothing behind it. The gate table below is
checked by [`tools/check-gate-policy.py`](../tools/check-gate-policy.py), which
reads the table, the scripts in `tools/` and the workflow files, and fails when
they disagree. A policy that only says "remember to update the table" decays
into a table that describes a repository which no longer exists.

## The measured picture

Measured on this branch (`dev` at `db95d550` plus this branch's commits),
the tree the table was last reconciled against:

| | |
|---|---|
| python tools in `tools/` | 7 files, 8 540 lines |
| of them, the `check-*.py` family | 4 files, 6 669 lines |
| workflows that run a python tool | 2: `ci.yml`, `docs.yml` |
| gates that block a build | 42 |
| gates that report and let the build pass | 0 |
| controls for compile-time gates | 1 (the compiled `check-tunit-analyzer-gate`) |
| reporters, helpers, libraries | 10 reporters, 10 helpers, 1 library |
| tools with a self-test | 52 |
| tools with a ratchet | 22 |
| tools with a floor | 31 |
| tools whose self-test no workflow ran before this change | 3 (`pack-validate.py`, `normalize-mtimes.py`, and `test-skips`, which this change compiles) |
| gates in a workflow that runs a script that is not in the tree | 0 |

The last two rows are the two gaps this policy closed on the way in, and both
were found by the checker rather than by reading: the checker was run against
the tree before the table was written, and it named them. The last row is now
0: `ci.yml`'s `public-api` job runs the compiled `check-public-api-resign` gate and
`tools/public-api-nonvacuity.sh`, both of which are in the tree (the job that
used to name the removed `check-public-api-abstractions.py` is the `public-api
freeze` one, and it was re-wired).

Two more gaps, found the same way and worth naming.

The policy was written against a base that had already moved, and the rebased
tree carried python tools the first draft of the table did not know about
(`check-reference-trimmer.py` and `msbuild-evaluation-cost.py` on the first
move, `check-dup-jscpd.py`, `check-no-test-sdk.py` and
`run-e2e-avalonia-shards.py` on the second). Those .py files are gone now:
the gates live in `tools/bin/harbor-gates-linux-x64`. The checker named each
of them on its first run against the new base, which is the whole argument
for having it.

The second move also found something worse: a squash that took the wrong side
of a conflict in `ci.yml` had dropped TWO gate jobs. The `reference-trimmer`
job and the `test-sdk-absent` job were gone from the workflow, so two gates
the tree still carried were not running at all. The checker named both: one
as `POLICY-MODE-GATE-NO-RUN`, the other as a python tool that no workflow
runs. A gate that is not wired cannot fire, and a gate that cannot fire is
what this policy is about.

## Why a gate is python or a committed binary

The reason is not speed. All the gates together take seconds, and moving
them to C# would add a restore, a build and a publish before each one.

The reason is **where the gate has to run**.

`ci.yml` ignores `**.md` and `docs/**` on purpose, for both `push` and
`pull_request`. A documentation-only pull request therefore never starts the
.NET build, and it gets a second workflow, `docs.yml`, which is deliberately
SDK-free. If those checks were C#, the check of the documentation of a pull
request that fixes the build would need the build to work first, and the
build is exactly what that pull request may have broken. The dependency would
be circular.

The same argument holds for the gates that run inside `ci.yml`: they read
files the build produced (a TRX, a publish log, a `.nupkg`) and files the
restore produced (`obj/project.assets.json`). They do not build anything. A
gate that needs the SDK cannot run on the pull request that fixes the build,
and a gate that needs a built Harbor cannot run on a documentation pull
request at all.

So a gate in this repository is a program that runs where Harbor does not
exist: no CLI, no product assemblies, no product dependencies, no NuGet
restore.

**A gate is one of two things**, and the difference is where its
implementation lives, not what it checks:

- a **python script** over files and artifacts: the standard library of a
  language every runner has, with nothing to build and nothing to install;
- a **compiled gate** of this repository: one multi-call binary
  (`harbor-gates <gate> [flags]`), one directory of Go sources per gate
  under `tools/gates/`, and the binary committed to the tree so that it
  runs where there is no SDK, no build of Harbor, and no python.

The reason for the second form is the first reason, sharpened: a gate has to
run where there is no SDK and no build, **and it must not cost the runner
minutes**. A committed binary satisfies both. The price is that a reviewer
cannot read a binary, and the answer to that is a machine check: the
`gates-binary` workflow rebuilds the binary from the sources in the same
tree and compares the bytes with the committed ones, so "the binary is what
the sources say" is a fact and not a promise.

Three reasons, and only three, put a check in `tools/` at all:

1. **It must run without the SDK and without a successful build.** The check
   has to work on the pull request that breaks the build.
2. **The invariant is a text or a tree, not a program.** A link, an anchor, a
   `file:line`, a markdown shape, a `.csproj`, a CI shard list, a TRX: all of
   them are files, and a file is read with a file API.
3. **It reads an artifact something else produced.** The test results, the
   publish log, the packed NuGet, the restore graph. The gate is a judge of an
   artifact, not a producer of one.

If none of the three holds, the check is a C# tool or a Roslyn analyzer, and
it belongs in the build, not in `tools/`.

## The docs single batch lane

All docs checks run in one workflow, `.github/workflows/docs.yml`. Commit
`87626512` removed the `paths:` filter on `pull_request`, so every pull
request starts this workflow and all six of its required status checks are
reported there: checker self-test, internal links, markdown lint, normative
citations, tree gates, and test project coverage. A docs change is checked
on its own pull request; it does not need a product slot to reach a gate.

The gates are batched, not split by product. The `tree` job runs every tree
gate in one command, `harbor-gates all`, and prints one table. The three
docs-specific gates (`check-md-links`, `md-lint`, and `check-doc-cites`)
scan the whole markdown tree in their own jobs. No workflow outside
`docs.yml` runs a markdown check. The full `docfx build` lives in
`docs-site.yml` behind a narrow trigger on the site inputs; that split is
by capability (SDK-free static checks versus an SDK build), not by product.

This note records the design for epic #1068. No gate, floor, or threshold
was changed here.

## What is not done in python

Anything that needs a type, a symbol, or a resolved semantic model. A text
scan over source code cannot prove a property of the program it describes,
and the gates that try are the ones that cry wolf.

The public-API freeze is the worked example, and it is a decision rather than
a complaint about python.

**What it was.** Two python text scanners, 1212 lines between them:
`tools/check-public-api.py` for the contract assembly and
`tools/check-public-api-abstractions.py` for the facade. They read the source
text and matched member declarations against a committed baseline.

**What it is.** `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.PublicApiAnalyzers` 5.6.0, attached to
the two frozen assemblies only, with `PrivateAssets=all`. `RS0016` (a public
symbol that the shipped file does not declare) and `RS0017` (a declared symbol
the code no longer has) fail the ordinary `build` job of `ci.yml`. The freeze
now lives where the freeze was always supposed to live: in the compile.

**Why the swap is not a downgrade.** The analyzer reads the compiler's symbol
table, so it sees what a line scan cannot:

- nullability (`RS0036` / `RS0037` / `RS0041`): `string` and `string?` are
  different signatures to the consumer, and a text scan saw only the word
  `string`;
- optional parameters (`RS0026` / `RS0027`), the compatibility rule that
  matters most when a surface is being frozen;
- a constructor that makes an inherited base `protected` (`RS0022`);
- implicit constructors and property accessors, which have no `public`
  keyword in the source at all;
- `const` and enum values, generic arity, and `init` accessors, all of which
  are part of a signature.

The inventory of analyzers and the decisions about them live in
[docs/ANALYZERS.md](ANALYZERS.md).

**What stayed in python, and why.** Half of the freeze cannot be a compile
gate: a change to the frozen surface has to be re-signed in the same commit,
and that is a question about a history, not about a tree. A compiler sees one
tree. So the re-signing rule is the compiled `check-public-api-resign` gate
([`tools/gates/check-public-api-resign/main.go`](../tools/gates/check-public-api-resign/main.go)),
and it is in the table below.

**How a compile-time gate proves it is not blind.** A python gate proves that
with `--self-test`. A compiler analyzer has no flag to run, so its
non-vacuity proof is a job:
[`tools/public-api-nonvacuity.sh`](../tools/public-api-nonvacuity.sh) builds a
throwaway project against the real analyzer and requires the build to fail
with `error RS0016`, then to pass once the row the analyzer asked for is
added, then to fail with `error RS0017` when the member is removed. The
lesson generalises: a gate that cannot be shown to fail is not a gate, and
how you show it depends on what the gate is made of.

## The rule of choice

Ask what the invariant needs:

| The invariant needs | The gate is |
|---|---|
| a link, an anchor, a heading shape, a `file:line` | a python text gate |
| a file tree, a `.csproj`, a CI list, a TRX, a baseline | a python file gate |
| the git history | a python gate over git plumbing |
| a resolved package graph | a python gate over `obj/project.assets.json` (a file) |
| a type, a symbol, a resolved overload set, a compiler's notion of visibility | a Roslyn analyzer, in the build |
| a duration | a benchmark, in [docs/BENCHMARKS.md](BENCHMARKS.md) |

The tie is broken by the question, not by the language the author is
comfortable in. A gate that asks "does this symbol exist?" is a compiler
question, and answering it with a regex is how a gate ends up reporting
findings that are not defects.

## What every gate owes

1. **A self-test with a planted control.** A gate that cannot fire is
   indistinguishable from a gate that is silent. The control is a real
   defect, and the self-test asserts both that the gate fails on it and what
   the gate says about it. A self-test that only asserts "exit code 1" is
   half a self-test: the message is the part a reader needs.
2. **A ratchet, and a floor that is not loosened.** Two different numbers,
   two different rules. A **baseline** (an exceptions file) is a ratchet: its
   rows may only shrink, because every row is a violation the tree is allowed
   to keep, and a new one is a new finding. A **floor** (`--min-*`) is the
   non-vacuity proof in numeric form: a scan that quietly narrowed must go red
   instead of reporting a clean tree. A floor is set AT the measured count,
   it is lowered in the same diff as the change that legitimately lowered the
   number, where a reviewer sees it, and it is RAISED when the measured count
   grows - a higher floor is stricter, and stricter is not a hole. What a
   floor may never do is be loosened to hide a regression.
3. **A deterministic exit.** The same tree gives the same exit code. No
   clock, no network, no randomness, no dependence on the machine.
4. **A message that names the violator.** "3 problems" costs the reader the
   whole run; the path, the line and the member cost nothing.
5. **No allow-list of files to skip, and no `continue-on-error`.** A skipped
   set is invisible at review time, and a gate that cannot fail is
   decoration.
6. **A header that says why it is python.** One line, near the top, in the
   form `Stdlib only - no pip, no network, no dotnet.` A **compiled** gate
   says why it is compiled instead, and its sources live under
   `tools/gates/<gate>/`, one directory per gate, with the standard library
   only and no external module.
7. **A compiled gate owes the repository its source, its bytes and its
   name.** The source is in `tools/gates/<gate>/`, the binaries are in
   `tools/bin/harbor-gates-linux-x64` and `tools/bin/harbor-gates-linux-arm64`,
   the hashes are in `tools/bin/SHA256SUMS`, and the name of the subcommand
   is the name of the directory. A pull request that changes one of them
   without the others is red, and the message names what to rebuild. There
   is never a python original and a compiled twin of the same gate in the
   tree: the twin is how a drifted pair is caught.

## What a gate must not do

- **Measure time.** A time threshold is a benchmark, and a benchmark belongs
  in [docs/BENCHMARKS.md](BENCHMARKS.md) with a methodology and a provenance.
  A gate that fails on a slow runner is a gate that gets switched off, and
  then it protects nothing.
- **Duplicate a gate that already exists.** Each of the four `check-*.py`
  tools answers a different question, and each states its question in its
  header so the next author can see the shape of what is already covered.
- **Require dotnet.** See the reason the gates are python at all.
- **Claim to be a gate while running advisory.** The table records the mode
  CI actually runs each tool in, and the policy checker fails when a row and
  its invocation disagree. The duplication gate used to be advisory while
  its removal programme ran; it blocks now, and the table says so.

## The gate table

Every python tool in `tools/` (6 files), plus the COMPILED gates, whose
sources are in `tools/gates/<gate>/` and whose binary is committed to the
tree. Five tools are run by a workflow; the other one is `md_gate.py`,
which is loaded by other tools rather than run. All of them are listed, because a tool
that is not listed is a tool nobody
reviews. The table records, for each one, the question
it answers, where its implementation lives, where it runs, whether it blocks a
build, whether it has a
self-test, the ratchet it holds, and the floors CI passes it. The table is
checked by `tools/check-gate-policy.py`, which fails when it stops describing
the tree: it names a tool the table does not list, and it names a table row
the tree does not have.

The modes are:

- **gate** - it fails a build.
- **advisory** - it reports and lets the build pass (`--warn-only`).
- **control** - it proves that a COMPILE-time gate is armed, so it runs the
  compiler. There are two of those: this one for the TUnit analyzer
  promotion, and `tools/public-api-nonvacuity.sh` for the public-API freeze.
- **reporter** - it prints and never fails.
- **helper** - a tool the pipeline uses, not a check of its own.
- **library** - imported by other tools, run by no workflow.

Two things the table says that are easy to miss:

- The compiled `msbuild-evaluation-cost` gate measures time, and it is NOT a
  gate. It
  is a reporter in a workflow of its own, and the policy's "a gate must not
  measure time" rule applies to gates alone: a measurement that fails a build
  on a slow runner is a gate that gets switched off, and a measurement that
  only reports belongs where this one is.
- `tools/ci-shard-slices.py` USED to have no self-test, for the same
  reason: it compared two things CI itself produced (the shard list
  against the slice list, two recordings of the same tape). Since the
  lists came from one source (issue #1800), the fixture is a desync
  planted in the tree rather than a flag, and the gate has one.

## The checker

[`tools/check-gate-policy.py`](../tools/check-gate-policy.py) is the rule
above, in code. It reads four sources - the table, the scripts in `tools/`,
the workflow files, and the list of the tree runner - and fails when they
disagree:

| Rule | What it catches |
|---|---|
| `POLICY-SCRIPT-UNDOCUMENTED` | a script CI runs that the table does not name |
| `POLICY-INVOCATION-DEAD` | a workflow running a script that is not in the tree |
| `POLICY-WORKFLOW-UNDECLARED` | a script run by a workflow the table does not name, or a workflow the table names that does not run it |
| `POLICY-JOB-UNKNOWN` | a job the table names that does not exist, or that does not run the script |
| `POLICY-MODE-GATE-NO-RUN` | a gate whose only CI use is its own self-test |
| `POLICY-MODE-GATE-WARN-ONLY` | a gate CI runs with `--warn-only` |
| `POLICY-MODE-ADVISORY-NOT-WARN-ONLY` | an advisory gate CI runs without `--warn-only` |
| `POLICY-SELFTEST-UNSUPPORTED` | a self-test flag the script does not accept, or a script that has one the table denies |
| `POLICY-SELFTEST-NOT-RUN` | a script with a self-test that no workflow ever runs |
| `POLICY-FLOORS-DIVERGE` | floors the table claims that CI does not pass, and floors CI passes that the script does not accept |
| `POLICY-BASELINE-MISSING` | a ratchet the table names that is not in the tree, or that the script never reads |
| `POLICY-HEADER-MISSING` | a gate whose header does not say why it is python |
| `POLICY-DOTNET-CALL` | a gate that shells out to dotnet |
| `POLICY-TIME-CALL` | a gate that measures time |
| `POLICY-SCRIPT-MISSING` | a row naming a script that is not in the tree |
| `POLICY-DUPLICATE-SCRIPT` | two rows for one script |
| `POLICY-TABLE-EMPTY` | a table that lost rows |
| `POLICY-ALL-LIST-UNREADABLE` | the list of the tree runner cannot be read, so the checker cannot tell which gates the runner runs |
| `POLICY-ALL-GATE-MISSING` | a gate of the list of the tree runner that is in neither `tools/gates/<name>/` nor `tools/<name>.py` |
| `POLICY-ALL-GATE-UNRUN` | a gate of the list of the tree runner that no workflow runs, neither directly nor through the runner |
| `POLICY-ALL-FLOORS-WEAKER` | the tree runner runs a gate with fewer floors than the gate's own job passes |

The rules it does not enforce are the ones no file can answer: what a gate
checks, that its message names the violator, that it has no allow-list, and
that it does not duplicate another gate. Those are reviewed by a human, and
the document says so rather than pretending otherwise.

## The tree runner is a runner, and the policy reads its list

`harbor-gates all` runs many gates in ONE command, and a workflow that
calls it runs every gate of its list that is compiled into the binary. That
makes the runner a THIRD source of truth about what CI runs, and the
checker has to read it - otherwise the table above describes a tree that
does not exist any more the moment a per-gate job is replaced by the runner.

**Where the list comes from.** The list is the Go source of the runner's
package, [`tools/gates/all/gates.go`](../tools/gates/all/gates.go), and NOT
the output of `harbor-gates all --list`:

- the committed binaries are LINUX binaries, and the checker has to run on
  any machine a developer sits at. A verdict that depends on the runner's
  operating system is a verdict that is green by never running on every
  machine that is not linux;
- `--list` prints a HUMAN table ("what each gate needs"). Recovering
  machine facts out of a human table couples the policy to a presentation
  format, and the format is the thing most likely to change for a reader's
  sake.

The source cannot drift from the binary: the binary IS the build of that
source, the `gates-binary` workflow rebuilds the binary from the sources in
the same tree and compares the bytes with the committed ones, and it
rebuilds and commits it on every push to `dev`. A pull request that changes
the list without rebuilding the binary is red there, not green here. And the
parse is LOUD: a list that cannot be read is a finding
(`POLICY-ALL-LIST-UNREADABLE`), never an empty list.

**What the runner really runs.** The binary must not need python, so the
runner runs the gates of the list that are COMPILED into it. A gate that is
still a python script is not one of them: it needs a workflow of its own,
and the local runner ([`tools/check-local.sh`](../tools/check-local.sh))
runs it with python3.

**The floors travel with the list.** The list carries the flags the
workflow passes each gate, and the checker compares them with the floors the
gate's own job passes. A runner that passed FEWER floors than another
runner would be a runner where the gate can be green because it scanned
nothing, and that is `POLICY-ALL-FLOORS-WEAKER`. The floors are therefore
checked BY THE LIST of gates and not by the lines of a workflow: a gate
whose job is deleted is still a gate with floors, and the runner is what
passes them now.

**What the table says about it.** For every gate the runner runs, the table
names the workflow and the job of the runner (`docs.yml`, `tree`) beside the
job that owns the gate, and the floors cell is the floors the runner passes
it. The `tree` job of `docs.yml` is the job that runs
`check-abstractions-contract`, `check-doc-facts`, `check-xml-doc-coverage`
and `gen-seam-graph`; their own jobs are gone, and the table says so.

**What it costs.** The runner's one command, measured from a green CI run,
spends 3 s on the compiled gates and 17 s on the whole job (issue #2135). The
number, its provenance and the split between compiled and python gates are in
[docs/BENCHMARKS.md](BENCHMARKS.md) §10.3.

Run it:

```bash
./tools/check-gate-policy.py --self-test
./tools/check-gate-policy.py --min-gates 38
```

Its own `--self-test` plants one defect per rule in a synthetic tree and
asserts that the rule fires, and that the same tree without the defect is
clean. A rule that cannot fire is indistinguishable from a rule that found
nothing, which is the failure every gate in this repository is tested
against. The tree runner has its own fixtures: a gate of its list that
nothing runs, a gate it runs without the floors of its own job, and a gate
of its list that is not in the tree at all.

## Adding a gate

1. Decide the question first, and put it in the header of the script. If the
   question needs a type or a symbol, it is an analyzer, not a gate here.
2. Write the failure path first: the planted control, the exit code, and the
   message. A gate whose message does not name the violator will be rewritten
   later, and the rewrite is the expensive part.
3. Give it a floor, and set the floor at the measured value. A floor below the
   measurement cannot tell "the tree got smaller" from "the matcher stopped
   matching".
4. Give it a ratchet, if the tree already violates the rule. The ratchet is a
   committed file that can only shrink.
5. Add it to the table above, and add its self-test to the `selftest` job of
   `docs.yml` (or to the job that runs it). The checker will say so if you
   forget, which is the point of the checker.
6. List it in [`tools/README.md`](../tools/README.md), whose first rule is
   that every script is listed.
7. Add the script to the `paths:` list of `docs.yml`, so that a pull request
   that edits the gate runs it. A gate made green by never running is the
   failure this repository has already paid for three times.

### Adding a COMPILED gate

A gate that costs more than a couple of seconds on every pull request is a
gate that should be compiled. The steps are the same as above, with the
implementation living in `tools/gates/<gate>/` instead of in
`tools/<gate>.py`:

1. The gate's name is the name of its directory and the name of its
   subcommand: `tools/gates/gen-seam-graph/` is `harbor-gates gen-seam-graph`.
2. The sources use the standard library only, and there is no `go.sum`: a
   gate that fetched something at run time could not run on a runner with no
   network.
3. The flags and the printed text are the ones the python original had.
   Compare the output of the two on the same tree BEFORE the original is
   deleted: the same exit code, the same text, the same verdicts.
4. `tools/build-gates.sh` builds the binary for both architectures and
   writes `tools/bin/SHA256SUMS`. Commit the binary with the sources: the
   binary IS the gate, and the sources without it are not a gate.
5. Delete the python original in the same pull request. A python original
   and a compiled twin of the same gate are two implementations of one
   gate, and they drift.
6. The workflow runs `tools/bin/harbor-gates-linux-x64 <gate> ...`, and the
   table row names that command and the source directory.

### 2.2 Build time

| Step | Duration |
|---|---|
| `dotnet restore` (cold, no cache) | ~6 s |
| `dotnet build` Debug (incremental, warm) | ~25 s |
| `dotnet build -c Release` (incremental, warm) | ~75 s |
| `dotnet build -c Release --no-incremental` (full) | ~120 s |

> These four rows are LOCAL numbers from the 2026-07-18 container of §1, on one
> developer machine. The CI compile is a different animal and is measured
> separately in §6.4: the NUKE `Compile` target takes 295-434 s on
> `ubuntu-24.04`, and the spread between runs is wider than the difference
> between the lane shapes.

| `contrib/apps/Harbor.App.Maui` | net10.0-windows | (skeleton — TBD) |

### 3.2 Publish folder size (JIT, framework-dependent)

Includes the app DLL + all NuGet deps + runtime deps. **This is what `dotnet publish` produces.**

| App | Publish folder size |
|---|---:|
| `Harbor.App.Cli` | **109 MB** |
| `Harbor.App.Avalonia` | ~140 MB (estimated; Avalonia + Skia + AvaloniaEdit) |
| `contrib/apps/Harbor.App.Wpf` | ~120 MB (estimated; Windows-only) |
| `contrib/apps/Harbor.App.Blazor` | ~115 MB (estimated; ASP.NET Core runtime) |
| `contrib/apps/Harbor.App.Maui` | ~150 MB (estimated; MAUI workload) |

> The 109 MB CLI publish folder is dominated by `Microsoft.Extensions.*`, `Spectre.Console`, `Spectre.Tui`, `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp` (Roslyn — 30+ MB alone for plugin compilation), and `MemoryPack` source-gen assemblies.

### 3.3 NativeAOT

**Status: publishable on the `fulltree` recipe since #1055s3** (record: `.github/aot-warning-baseline.txt`, gate: #413; measured binary + workload in §4.4). What unblocked it: the in-process CS-source plugin pipeline (`Harbor.Plugins.{Compilation,Instantiation,Registration,Storage}`) left the CLI process — the default route is the out-of-process host — so Roslyn (`Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp`) is no longer in the trim graph. No suppression was added. Still true: the `minimal` recipe (`HARBOR_MINIMAL=true`, the stripped profile) does not compile (11 x CS0234, see the baseline file), and the contrib Spectre renderers stay out of the AOT graph via build flags.

**Roadmap remainder:** the `minimal` profile plus dropping in-process Roslyn and Spectre reflection for the main process was the v0.9 two-process milestone — the Roslyn half of that landed via #1055. Measured AOT binary size: 29 MB self-contained (§4.4), against the 14–20 MB estimate below.

To reproduce the measured publish today (needs the AOT toolchain: `clang`, `lld`, `binutils`, `zlib1g-dev`):
```bash
dotnet publish apps/Harbor.App.Cli -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained true -p:HarborWithAot=true
# Green in CI (the `aot-publish` job); the published binary runs version/help/providers. Full recipe in tools/measure-aot-workload.sh.
```

### 3.4 Framework-dependent vs Self-contained

| Mode | CLI publish size | When to use |
|---|---:|---|
| Framework-dependent (default) | 109 MB | Dev / power users with .NET 10 installed |
| Self-contained `--self-contained` | ~85 MB + ~75 MB runtime = **160 MB** | End users without .NET |
| Self-contained + `PublishSingleFile` | ~85 MB single binary + ~75 MB runtime files | Distribution |
| Self-contained + `PublishTrimmed` | ~50 MB | Experimental — breaks Spectre.Console reflection |
| NativeAOT (`fulltree`, measured §4.4) | 29 MB self-contained | Production target |

## 4. Runtime metrics

### 4.1 Cold start

Measured as wall-clock time from process spawn (`dotnet run --no-build -c Release --project apps/Harbor.App.Cli -- --version`) to first byte of stdout.

| Run | Duration |
|---|---:|
| Run 1 | 966 ms |
| Run 2 | 887 ms |
| Run 3 | 1 032 ms |
| **Median** | **966 ms** |

Breakdown (estimated):
- `dotnet` host startup + JIT: ~300 ms
- Assembly load (`Harbor.App.Cli.dll` + deps): ~200 ms
- `HostBuilder` DI wiring: ~150 ms
- Provider/tool/agent registry construction: ~200 ms
- `IHost.StartAsync`: ~100 ms

> AOT target: <100 ms cold start (10x improvement) once NativeAOT is supported.

### 4.2 RSS (resident set size)

**Could not measure accurately in sandbox** — the `harbor ask "say hi"` command requires API key + provider, which fails in the sandbox.

Estimates based on .NET 10 baseline + Harbor deps:
- CLI idle (after `--version` exits): N/A (process exits too fast)
- CLI active (running prompt): ~80-120 MB (dominated by Spectre.Console + Roslyn plugin host)
- Avalonia app (window open): ~150-200 MB (Avalonia + Skia + AvaloniaEdit)
- WPF app: ~120-180 MB (AvalonEdit + AvalonDock)
- Blazor Server: ~100-150 MB (Kestrel + SignalR)

> The previous "28 MB RSS idle" claim was for a Debug build of the old `Harbor.Cli` (pre-split) running `--version` and exiting immediately — not a realistic number for an interactive session.

### 4.3 GC pressure

Not yet measured with `dotnet-counters`. The `InMemoryEventBus`, `UiStore` (now lock-free CAS), and `AgentLoop` (uses `StringBuilderPool`, `ArrayPool`) are designed for low allocation. BenchmarkDotNet microbenchmarks below quantify the hot paths.

### 4.4 JIT vs NativeAOT scripted workload (#411) — both halves measured

Harness: `tools/measure-jit-workload.sh` + `tools/measure-aot-workload.sh` (offline CLI verbs `--version` / `--help` / `providers`, N=7, median + spread — never a single number; same verbs, same N, same table shape); CI runner `.github/workflows/meas-jit-aot.yml` (measurement only, not a gate). Full logs are the `jit-workload-log` / `aot-workload-log` artifacts of the runs linked below.

Measured (JIT) — run [37935894413](https://github.com/refusedguy/Harbor-Harness/actions/runs/37935894413), 2026-10-09, commit `eebc9be3`, AMD EPYC 7763 (4 vCPU, x86_64), Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, .NET SDK 10.0.401, framework-dependent Release, apphost-driven (no `dotnet` muxer in path).

| Verb | Median | Min | Max | Spread | RSS peak (median) | RSS peak (max) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `--version` | 138 ms | 133 ms | 194 ms | 1.46x | 43 124 KB | 43 248 KB |
| `--help` | 134 ms | 131 ms | 143 ms | 1.09x | 43 336 KB | 43 336 KB |
| `providers` | 459 ms | 454 ms | 533 ms | 1.17x | 96 440 KB | 96 448 KB |

Wall = process spawn-to-exit per verb; RSS = `ru_maxrss` peak (KB). Publish dir: 51 MB (53 159 039 bytes); apphost binary: 40 MB (framework-dependent — needs an installed .NET runtime). The `providers` verb is the DI-heavy one (full `HostBuilder` + provider registry) and the closest proxy here to real startup: ~459 ms JIT, ~94 MB RSS peak.

Measured (AOT) — run [38110959202](https://github.com/refusedguy/Harbor-Harness/actions/runs/38110959202), 2026-10-11, commit `1ef2e522` (PR #1151 head; delta vs dev is harness files only, no production code), same machine class — AMD EPYC 7763 (4 vCPU, x86_64), Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, .NET SDK 10.0.401 — self-contained linux-x64, verbatim #413 recipe (`-p:HarborWithAot=true`; record: `.github/aot-warning-baseline.txt`, status=published).

| Verb | Median | Min | Max | Spread | RSS peak (median) | RSS peak (max) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `--version` | 18 ms | 17 ms | 25 ms | 1.48x | 29 220 KB | 29 220 KB |
| `--help` | 19 ms | 17 ms | 24 ms | 1.38x | 29 220 KB | 29 220 KB |
| `providers` | 58 ms | 55 ms | 62 ms | 1.12x | 35 544 KB | 35 544 KB |

Wall and RSS as above. Publish dir: 41 MB (41 868 731 bytes); binary: 29 MB, self-contained (no shared framework needed). Comparability note: JIT and AOT columns come from different days but the same machine class, OS, and SDK; the same dispatch re-ran the JIT leg and its wall-clock medians (139 / 133 / 420 ms) reproduce the committed JIT column within spread.

Answer to the #411 decision question, quantified: AOT buys **7.7x / 7.1x / 7.9x** spawn-to-exit on `--version` / `--help` / `providers`, **1.5x** RSS on the light verbs (43 → 29 MB) and **2.7x** on the DI-heavy verb (94 → 35 MB), with a 29 MB self-contained binary replacing a 40 MB framework-dependent apphost. The §4.1 target (<100 ms cold start) is met as a measurement on all three verbs (18 / 19 / 58 ms). On this workload the trade of #48 answers **yes**: the startup win is measured, and the thing given up for it — in-process Roslyn plugin compile — already has its default out-of-process route (#1055, 0.021 ms mean loopback dispatch). What this table still does not cover, for either mode: time-to-first-frame, steady-state allocs/op, and input-latency p50/p95 from the #411 criteria — spawn-to-exit plus RSS peak is the evidence that exists.

### 4.5 Interactive render metrics: measured vs not yet measured (#2221)

The terminal-interactivity metrics that kitty and Ghostty publish are not all in this file yet. This subsection records the boundary honestly. Every number in Table 1 is copied from a measurement that already has a run and a machine in this document. No estimate is written in place of a missing measurement. Where a metric has no run, the method to produce it is described and the item stays open.

Table 1: already measured, evidence in this file

| Metric | Value | Provenance | Machine and method |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spawn-to-exit, JIT `--version` / `--help` / `providers` | 138 / 134 / 459 ms median | §4.4, Actions run 37935894413, 2026-10-09, commit `eebc9be3` | AMD EPYC 7763, 4 vCPU, Ubuntu 24.04.5, .NET SDK 10.0.401, Release apphost |
| Spawn-to-exit, AOT same three verbs | 18 / 19 / 58 ms median | §4.4, Actions run 38110959202, 2026-10-11, commit `1ef2e522` | Same machine class, self-contained linux-x64, #413 recipe |
| RSS peak, JIT light / DI-heavy verb | 43 MB / 96 MB | §4.4, run 37935894413 | `ru_maxrss` median |
| RSS peak, AOT light / DI-heavy verb | 29 MB / 35 MB | §4.4, run 38110959202 | `ru_maxrss` median |
| Hinted cell-diff, 120x500 live chat timeline | 0.317 ms | Renderer-moat probes, 2026-08-31, `RendererMoatPerfTests` | Linux x64, .NET 10 Release JIT, discarding backend, no tty I/O |
| Full frame, solve+paint+hinted diff+encode | 0.805 ms | Same probe | Same |
| Armed post-fx glow frame | 0.671 ms | Same probe, within noise of the 0.805 ms base | Same |
| Steady-frame allocations, 2 000 hinted frames | 0 B | Same probe | Same |

Spawn-to-exit and cold start are not time-to-first-frame. The §4.1 median of 966 ms is wall-clock from process spawn to the first stdout byte of `--version`, not to the first rendered frame on a PTY. None of the Table 1 values may be relabeled as TTFF, input latency, or steady-state allocs/op.

Table 2: requested metrics with no run yet, tasks and not estimates

| Metric | Status | Instrument and method | Acceptance when added |
|---|---|---|---|
| Time-to-first-frame, JIT and AOT | NOT MEASURED | PTY harness with `HARBOR_TUI=cellforge`; timestamp process spawn and the first `WriteAsync` surfaced through `EngineStageCounters`; report spawn to the first byte of the first frame, not spawn to exit | N >= 7, median plus spread, both modes, run id and machine recorded |
| Input latency p50/p95/p99 | NOT MEASURED | Timestamp the `InputEvent` in `TerminalInputSource` and the first frame whose diff carries its effect (caret move or prompt delta); measure pacer hysteresis separately so `CommitTickPacer` does not shift p95 | Report the distribution, not the mean; keyboard-to-screen analog of kitty |
| Frame budget distribution | NOT MEASURED | Per-frame `solve+paint+diff+encode` over the same 120x500 live timeline as `RendererMoatPerfTests`, with a separate line for armed glow | p50/p95/p99, not only the 0.805 ms mean |
| Steady-state allocs/op | NOT MEASURED | `GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread` or BenchmarkDotNet around each scenario: stream token, tool-call delta, spinner tick, mouse wheel, paste, resize, overlay open/close | Bytes per operation per scenario; a 0 B/op claim only where measured |
| Damage ratio | NOT MEASURED | Count cells emitted against screen area (cols x rows) via `DiffEngine.HintArea()`; count hint hits versus full-scan fallback at the 25% threshold | Emitted/area ratio and fallback frequency, with the run recorded |
| GC pause / Gen0 over a 30 s stream | NOT MEASURED | `dotnet-counters` against a 30-second stream, Gen0 count and pause histogram; closes the §4.3 gap | Counter output attached and run id recorded |
| AOT versus JIT at steady state | NOT MEASURED | Same PTY workload in both binaries, compare p95 frame time and Gen0 count | p95 and GC in both modes; no claim inferred from startup numbers |
| Parser throughput, bytes/s | NOT MEASURED | Feed a bootstrap ANSI stream into `EscapeSequenceParser` with rendering disabled, count input bytes per second | Comparable to kitty throughput with the explicit caveat that this is a parser, not a terminal emulator |

Verdict on "fast as Rust": unconfirmed. What this file proves is a zero-allocation cell-diff core (0 B over 2 000 frames), a 0.317 ms hinted diff against a 16 ms budget, and a 7 to 8x startup win under AOT. It does not yet prove time-to-first-frame, p95 input latency, or steady-state allocs/op in the form kitty and Ghostty publish. Until Table 2 has recorded runs, the defensible claim is that the engine has measured microbenchmarks and the architectural preconditions, not parity with Rust-grade terminal performance.

This subsection changes no portable threshold and no CI gate. It is documentation only.

### 5.3 Event-bus + IPC delivery split (#408) ⏳ not yet measured

Before #408 the bus rows were one blended number per class, so "event bus throughput" silently
